IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON INSTRUMENTATION AND MEASUREMENT, VOL. 73, 2024 5502414
Design and Performance Analysis for Indoor
Visible Light Positioning With Single LED and
Single-Tilted-Rotatable PD
Zhenyu Wang , Zhonghua Liang , Senior Member, IEEE, Ren Liu , Xunuo Li , and Hui Li
Abstract— In recent years, single-LED-based visible light posi-
tioning (VLP) systems have been developed because of their
low complexity, simple conﬁguration, and feasibility for indoor
application scenarios. In this article, ﬁrst, we describe the
system model of the single-tilted-rotatable-photodetector (STRP)-
based receiver in single-LED scenario considering the ﬁrst-order
reﬂection signal. Then, we derive the Cramer–Rao lower bound
(CRLB) of the positioning error for the received signal strength
(RSS)-based positioning system using the discussed model and
select proper inclination and rotation angles according to the
derived CRLB. In addition, we analyze the least-square (LS)
positioning method and propose an improved gray wolf optimiza-
tion (IGWO)-based localization algorithm with the assistance
of the LS method. Finally, the proposed LS-IGWO positioning
algorithm has been evaluated in terms of accuracy and latency via
software simulations and ﬁeld tests. Simulation and experiment
results show that using the RSS-based positioning model, the
proposed LS-IGWO algorithm can achieve centimeter-level posi-
tioning accuracy and performs best compared with the original
LS, the original GWO, single IGWO, pure LS-GWO, and the
existing ﬁngerprint method.
Index Terms— Cramer–Rao lower bound (CRLB), gray wolf
optimization (GWO), least square (LS), received signal strength
(RSS), single LED, visible light positioning (VLP).
I. INTRODUCTION
N
OWADAYS, due to the demand for indoor location-
based services, indoor positioning systems (IPSs) have
gradually become a research hotspot and attracted plenty
of enterprises and institutions to develop commercial prod-
ucts [1]. IPSs aim at real-time and precise tracking of the
position of users or objects in many complicated indoor envi-
ronments, but the global positioning system (GPS) is difﬁcult
to achieve that purpose due to its limitations [2]. Therefore,
IPSs based on indoor wireless signals, such as Wi-Fi [3],
[4], Bluetooth [5], radio frequency identiﬁcation (RFID) [6],
ultrawideband (UWB) [7], and visible light communication
(VLC) [8], [9], have been well developed in recent years.
Among them, VLC-based IPSs have been paid much attention

because of their high transmission rate, energy conservation,
weak electromagnetic interference, long lifespan, and low
cost [2].
VLC-based positioning systems usually use one or more
LED lamps as the transmitter to help the users get their
position. Most existing visible light positioning (VLP) sys-
tems use multiple LEDs to achieve high-accuracy positioning
because of its strong stability, wide lighting range, and simple
receiver structure. However, for a small room, using one LED
is sufﬁcient to achieve lighting, so it is a more cost-efﬁcient
solution to deploy single LED. On the one hand, for single-
LED-based VLP systems, compared with the multi-LEDs, the
hardware signal processing delay at the receiver is much lower,
because it does not need to use multiple access protocols to
distinguish signals from different LEDs, and that improves
the real-time positioning performance. In addition, single-LED
systems can avoid the design of LED’s layout, the interference
between LEDs, and the waste of light resources, making it
more convenient for the VLP implementation [10]. On the
other hand, the designs of high-precision positioning algorithm
and appropriate receiver are still challenging for single-LED
scenarios. Therefore, in practice, it is necessary to decide to
use one or multiple LEDs according to the actual size of
the measured room and performance requirements, and VLP
systems with single LED can be considered as a cost-efﬁcient
IPS solution for a small room.
In VLP systems, received signal strength (RSS) detected by
photodetectors (PDs) is more widely used, because they do not
need additional synchronization maintenance or high-precision
image acquisition devices. Therefore, RSS-PD-based VLP
systems can be considered a low-cost solution to the indoor
positioning problem [11]. In [12], the impact of the multipath
reﬂection signal on positioning performance was analyzed
for RSS-PD-based indoor VLP systems. Moreover, in [13]
and [14], the performance limits of LED-based positioning
and orientation systems were studied in non-line-of-sight
(NLOS) environments. Fingerprint and least-square (LS)-
based VLP algorithms considering multipath reﬂection were
studied in [15] and [16], respectively. However, these studies
are all implemented in multi-LED scenarios. For single-LED
scenes, there are few related studies, so it is necessary to
analyze the performance of the VLP system in this case.
At the receiver, PDs or image sensors (ISs) are commonly
taken as the device for sensing optical signals [17]. In the

presence of single-LED-based VLP system, a receiver with
multi-PDs, ISs, or single-rotatable PD is mainly utilized to
estimate the position of the target node (TN). In [18], multiple
PDs were used in single-LED-based IPS. The receiver is
composed of a horizontal PD and two tilted PDs. In [19],
the CMOS-made IS was used to estimate the TN’s position
by ﬁnding the camera pose, and they designed a positioning
algorithm for an arbitrarily tilted smartphone. Liu et al. [10]
designed a receiver with a rotatable PD in single-LED scenario
and then proposed a VLP algorithm based on machine learning
(ML) methods concerning the ﬁrst-order reﬂection of the
optical power. In [20], a receiver equipped with a single-
tilted-rotatable PD (STRP) was implemented, and accordingly,
the ﬁngerprint positioning using K -nearest-neighbor (KNN)
method was designed. The experiment was implemented in a
600 × 600 × 1135 mm
3
indoor environment, and the average
positioning error of 25 TNs is less than 25 mm.
However, some challenges need to be addressed in the exist-
ing studies for single-LED scenarios. For example, in [10], the
receiver carrying PD is equipped with a long rotation arm,
and thus, it is not suitable for system integration, and the
ﬁngerprint-based positioning algorithm proposed in [10] has
slightly higher complexity. Small-size receivers are designed
in [18] and [20], but they did not consider the effect of
reﬂected signals. Therefore, the performance of positioning
algorithms presented in [18] and [20] is limited in indoor
NLOS environments. Furthermore, there are few studies about
single-LED single-PD (SLSP)-based IPS, and the performance
of ﬁngerprint-based localization algorithms usually deterio-
rates when considering the LED orientation. To address the
above problems, we further analyze the STRP-based receiver
designed in [20] for the SLSP scenario and, accordingly,
propose an improved gray wolf optimization (IGWO) posi-
tioning algorithm with the assistance of the LS method
(LS-IGWO). The performance of the proposed LS-IGWO
positioning algorithm is veriﬁed via software simulations and
ﬁeld tests. Our major contributions are summarized as follows.
1) We derive the Cramer–Rao lower bound (CRLB) of the
positioning error using the STRP proposed in [20] con-
sidering the ﬁrst-order reﬂection signal for single-LED
scenario and analyze how to select proper inclination
and rotation angles.
2) The original LS positioning method based on SRTP is
derived in single-LED scenario, and then, we design an
initial population generation strategy based on the result
of the LS method.
3) The GWO algorithm is implemented in single-LED
scenario to estimate the position of the TN using the
ﬁngerprint database generated by the STRP-based VLC
channel model.
4) We introduce three improvement mechanisms, namely,
nonlinear convergence factor, weighted update strat-
egy, and mutation of the head wolf into the proposed
LS-IGWO algorithm to address the local optimum prob-
lems.
5) We evaluate the performances of the original LS [21],
the original GWO [22], single IGWO, pure LS-GWO,
the ﬁngerprint method [20], and the proposed LS-IGWO
Fig. 1. VLC system diagram.
positioning algorithms in terms of positioning accuracy
and latency.
The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II
introduces the VLC channel modeling using Lambert radiation
source, STRP-based receiver, and CRLB of the positioning
error in the implemented positioning system. Section III
derives the original LS method and describes the proposed
LS-IGWO positioning algorithm. Section IV analyzes the
performance of the proposed LS-IGWO positioning algorithm
using software simulation. Section V presents the ﬁeld test
of our proposed method. Finally, our works are concluded in
Section VI.

For the implementation of an actual VLP system, the STRP
model shown in Fig. 4 is placed on a rotatable platform with
precise angle scale so as to achieve RSS values detection
for different rotation angles. The rotatable platform can be
controlled electromechanically, remotely, or manually. In the
ﬁeld experiment, we use a manual rotatable platform to
achieve this function. The speciﬁc experimental facilities will
be introduced in Section V.

C. Proposed LS-IGWO Positioning Method
For the GWO algorithm used in the abovementioned VLP
system, three problems need to be addressed: ﬁtness calcu-
lation, initial population generation, and local optimum. The
solutions to these problems are stated as follows.
1) Artiﬁcial RSS Database: For (49), the calculation of
P
(c)
is inconvenient, because a large amount of reﬂected
optical power in (30) will increase the complexity of the
GWO iteration. Therefore, in the ofﬂine phase, we use (30)
to generate an artiﬁcial database shown in Table II. When
we need to calculate an individual’s ﬁtness, we can use its
position to obtain the theoretical values of the N received
powers prestored in the database.
In fact, when the RSS parameter estimation model is simple
enough, there is no need to establish a database, such as
Table II. We only use the database to accelerate the simulation
of the GWO algorithm instead of proposing a ﬁngerprint-based
positioning method. In our ﬁeld test shown in Section V,
we will use a newly measured RSS model for localization
in small areas.
2) Initial Population Generation Strategy Based on LS: To
improve the convergence accuracy, the estimated position of
the TN by LS method is used to generate the initial population
in this article. As shown in Fig. 9, the four vertices of the

IV. SIMULATION RESULTS
In this section, we evaluate the performance of the proposed
LS-IGWO positioning algorithm in terms of accuracy and
latency when LED is placed horizontally and tilted on the
ceiling, respectively. During the simulations, the averaged
positioning error (APE) is obtained from 576 different posi-
tions uniformly distributed in the simulated room illustrated
in Fig. 2, and for all the positioning algorithms related to
GWO, the number of wolves and iterations is set to 25 and
10, respectively. The VLC signals shown in Fig. 5 are used in
the simulations, and all the parameters about VLP are listed
in Table I.
Fig. 10. Positioning error distribution of the original LS method using the
STRP-based receiver.
Fig. 11. Probability of enclosing the TN using the generated area for different
SNR values.
A. Case in Which LED Is Vertically Downward
Fig. 10 shows the positioning performance of the original
LS [21] positioning algorithm for each investigated TN in the
whole room when SNR = 20 dB. It can be seen that due to
the inﬂuence of reﬂected optical power near the edge area, the
positioning accuracy becomes worse. The average positioning
error in the edge and center area of the room is 0.80 and
0.16 m, respectively, and the maximum positioning error is
1.76 m (we consider that the area in which the horizontal
and vertical coordinates range from 1 to 4 m is the central
area, while the rest is the edge area). Therefore, neglecting the
NLOS components is unreasonable, and thus, the performance
of the original LS method is unsatisfactory when it is used
directly.
Fig. 11 shows the probability that the area generated by (55)
and (56) can enclose the TN at each investigated position for
different SNR values when D = 2 m. We see that due to
the dependence on the performance of the LS method and the
noise of the received optical power, the generated area may
not contain TN for low SNR values. However, when SNR >
14 dB, the region can enclose TN with a probability of nearly
100%, so the improvement for the original GWO in terms of
Authorized licensed use limited to: Universite de Versailles St Quentin. Downloaded on September 03,2026 at 11:06:43 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply.
WANG et al.: DESIGN AND PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS FOR INDOOR VISIBLE LIGHT POSITIONING 5502414
Fig. 12. Positioning error distribution of the proposed LS-IGWO positioning
algorithm.
Fig. 13. CDF of the positioning error for the six investigated positioning
algorithms.
positioning accuracy would make more sense for higher SNR
values.
Fig. 12 shows the overall positioning performance of the
proposed LS-IGWO localization algorithm under the same
conditions as Fig. 10. We see that compared with Fig. 10,
the overall positioning error has signiﬁcantly decreased by
using the proposed LS-IGWO algorithm. According to our
observation, the positioning error in the edge and center
areas of the room has decreased by 92.13% and 73.42%,
respectively, and the maximum positioning error drops to
0.758 m.
Fig. 13 shows the positioning error’s cumulative distribution
function (cdf) of the original LS [21], original GWO [22],
GWO with the initialization strategy shown in (55) and (56)
(pure LS-GWO), GWO using the improvement mechanism
given by (57)–(60) (single IGWO), the proposed LS-IGWO,
and the ﬁngerprint method in [20] for SNR = 20 dB. We see
that the positioning error of the proposed LS-IGWO algorithm
is closest to the theoretical CRLB boundary, and about 92.19%
of the positioning error values are within 0.1131 m for the
Fig. 14. APE of the six investigated positioning algorithms for different
SNR values.
proposed LS-IGWO algorithm. Compared with the original
GWO algorithm, the positioning accuracy has improved by
about 59.36% using the proposed LS-IGWO algorithm.
Fig. 14 shows the comparison of the six investigated algo-
rithms in terms of the APE under different SNR values. We see
that the proposed LS-IGWO positioning algorithm has better
positioning accuracy than other algorithms at all the investi-
gated SNR values. Because the original LS and the ﬁngerprint
localization algorithms in [20] do not consider the inﬂuence
of the reﬂected optical signal, their positioning performance
is unsatisfactory. In addition, we can also see that the single
IGWO and pure LS-GWO perform better than the original
GWO [22]. Therefore, the initial population generating strat-
egy (55) and (56) and the improvement mechanisms (57)–(60)
are effective for the proposed LS-IGWO algorithm.
Fig. 15 shows the time consumption of the six investi-
gated algorithms. We see that compared with the original
LS [21] and GWO [22] algorithms, the proposed LS-IGWO
algorithm can enhance positioning accuracy at a limited cost
of time complexity. For the proposed LS-IGWO algorithm,
the combination of the original LS and GWO methods in
conjunction with the improved strategies increases the time
complexity. Therefore, the proposed LS-IGWO algorithm can
be considered for the scenarios that are insensitive to time
delay. Because the original LS [21], original GWO [22],
single IGWO, pure LS-GWO, and the proposed LS-IGWO
algorithms do not require online ﬁngerprint database matching,
the positioning latency is much lower than the ﬁngerprint
method in [20] using KNN.
Fig. 16 provides the APE and positioning latency of the pro-
posed LS-IGWO algorithm with different numbers of wolves
when SNR = 20 dB. We see that when the number of pop-
ulations is more than 25, the improvement in the positioning
error becomes smaller and smaller, so we use 25 populations
in our simulations. As the number of populations increases,
the positioning accuracy becomes better, but the positioning
delay also becomes larger. Therefore, we can adjust the pop-
ulation size according to the actual positioning requirements

effectiveness of the proposed LS-IGWO positioning algorithm.

The root-mean-square error (RMSE) between the measured
RSS samples and the above two model curves in Fig. 23
are shown in Table III. We see that the ﬁtted model (65) is
generally more accurate than the Lambert radiation model used
in the previous simulation. Actually, in practical positioning
scenarios, not all LED lamps can be modeled as a standard
Lambert radiation source because of the various shapes of
lamps and indoor facilities. We usually need to obtain the
RSS model based on actual measured RSS samples and
mathematical tools, such as curve ﬁtting. Therefore, in the
practical localization, we recommend the newly derived RSS
model (65) instead of the original simulation model. When
considering the complex NLOS environments, we can update

Therefore, by using (65), we can construct the parameter
estimation model, such as (37), and the TN’s position can
be estimated by the positioning algorithm demonstrated in
Section III. For good robustness, it would be better to regularly
update the RSS model based on changes in indoor environ-
ments, such as furniture layout and ambient light.

lation time of all the GWO-based localization algorithms is
about 9.7 ms. Due to the simplicity of the RSS parameter
estimation model established by (65), there is no need to
establish a ﬁngerprint database, such as previous simulations,
to improve computational efﬁciency.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this article, we evaluated the theoretical performance of
an existing STRP-based receiver in the SLSP scenarios and
then proposed an LS-IGWO-based VLP algorithm to mitigate
the impact of the ﬁrst-order reﬂection optical signals. Accord-
ing to the derived CRLB of the positioning error, the proper
angles of inclination and rotation are selected. Simulation and
ﬁeld test results show that for different LED orientations,
the proposed LS-IGWO positioning algorithm has higher
positioning accuracy and stronger stability than the original
LS [21], the original GWO [22], single IGWO, pure LS-
GWO, and the existing ﬁngerprint positioning algorithm [20].
Therefore, the proposed LS-IGWO positioning algorithm with
STRP is effective and feasible and can be considered as a
competitive solution for SLSP-based IPS.
In our future work, we will focus on developing RSS-based
VLP systems, including more accurate single-LED-based
positioning schemes, real-time positioning algorithms, simul-
taneous positioning and orientation for the receiver, LED
orientation estimation, and system implementation for 6G
applications.
